questions.question: Which statement correctly separates the two service-mesh planes?
options: The control plane forwards every application request, while the data plane stores policy files
The control plane distributes desired state, while the data plane handles and enforces application traffic
The data plane manages only dashboards, while the control plane runs application code
Both planes must synchronously approve every request
questions.explanation: The control plane configures data-plane enforcement points. Keeping it out of the synchronous application path lets an accepted configuration continue to serve when the control plane is briefly unavailable.

questions.question: In the lesson topology, the control plane fails after both enforcement points accepted usable configuration. What is the expected immediate result?
options: Existing requests can use the last accepted state, but new discovery, identity, or policy changes may be affected
Every application request must immediately bypass all policy
The Orders workload automatically becomes the new control plane
Mutual TLS permanently disables itself
questions.explanation: The modeled data plane can continue enforcing its accepted state. Operators still need to restore the control plane before trusting configuration or identity changes.

questions.question: What does mutual TLS provide between participating mesh peers?
options: Encryption and peer authentication, but not permission to perform every operation
Business-level authorization for every database row
Exactly-once execution of retried writes
Automatic correctness of application responses
questions.explanation: Mutual TLS protects transport and authenticates identities. Authorization policy and application logic still decide what an authenticated caller may do.

questions.question: A route receives 1,000 requests per second and permits two retries. What maximum attempt rate can the policy allow when every eligible attempt fails and the deadline permits all attempts?
options: 1,000 attempts per second
2,000 attempts per second
3,000 attempts per second
4,000 attempts per second
questions.explanation: Two retries allow one initial attempt plus two additional attempts. The failure-path ceiling is therefore 1,000 x 3 = 3,000 attempts per second.

questions.question: A small system only needs host and path routing for one public API plus normal Kubernetes service discovery. What is the smallest modeled fit?
options: A service mesh across every workload
Kubernetes Services plus a gateway
A second control plane for each application
Per-request mutual TLS certificates issued by the client
questions.explanation: A gateway and Kubernetes Services cover the selected edge-routing and discovery requirements without adding a mesh data plane to internal calls.

questions.question: The internal-identity requirement fits a mesh, but no team owns policy review, upgrades, certificates, or incidents. What should happen next?
options: Enroll every workload immediately because feature fit is enough
Ignore operating readiness and rely on default settings
Build ownership, choose a managed path, or narrow the pilot before broad rollout
Move authorization into source IP allowlists
questions.explanation: Technical coverage does not remove the new failure domain. A mesh needs explicit ownership and a bounded adoption path before it becomes part of every request.

questions.question: Which claim can proxy telemetry support most directly?
options: A payment was captured exactly once
An order contains the correct business data
The request rate, response class, latency, and retry attempts observed at the network boundary
A database invariant can never be violated
questions.explanation: The data plane sees network behavior. Business correctness still requires application and domain evidence.
